query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive framework that independently calculates lattice thermal conductivity (via phonon dynamics captured by MD with machine-learned force fields) and electronic thermal conductivity (via an ab initio electronic structure and Boltzmann transport approach using deformation potential theory) will predict the individual contributions in HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional models that conflate the two, resulting in a total thermal conductivity prediction within approximately ±15% of experimental values and a 30–50% improvement in accuracy over earlier approaches.
generation.material_initial_state: Defect‐free, bulk HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with controlled impurity levels (e.g., oxygen <1 wt%).
generation.intervention: Apply the new predictive framework that separately computes lattice thermal conductivity using Green–Kubo MD with on-the-fly machine-learned force fields and electronic conductivity using DFT-based electronic structure calculations (including SOC) coupled with Boltzmann transport and deformation potential theory.
generation.conditions: Simulations and experiments performed over a temperature range from 300 K to 1200 K under conditions mimicking perfect crystal behavior; sample conditions with minimal extrinsic defects and controlled oxygen content.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale mass and force-constant fluctuations that dominate phonon scattering, while electronic conduction is mediated by free charge carriers whose relaxation times are governed by deformation potential effects.
generation.mechanism: By decoupling the phonon (lattice) and electron (charge) contributions, the framework accurately captures the dominant scattering mechanisms in each channel. The method uses detailed MD simulations to resolve the full phonon dynamics (including higher-order anharmonic effects) and advanced ab initio calculations to treat electron scattering separately, thereby avoiding the averaging errors inherent to conflated models.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predicted lattice and electronic thermal conductivities will, when added, yield a total thermal conductivity that aligns with experimental benchmarks (10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures) within ±15% error. This represents a 30–50% improvement in predictive accuracy compared to traditional approaches that do not distinguish between the two contributions.
generation.baseline: Conventional analytical and simulation methods that conflate lattice and electronic contributions, which typically show larger discrepancies from measured data (errors of 25% or more), especially given the complexities introduced by force-constant disorder.
generation.boundary: Applicability is limited to the temperature range of 300–1200 K and to samples with low defect and oxygen content; predictions may be less reliable at very low temperatures (<200 K) where electron-phonon interactions present additional challenges.
generation.uncertainty: While the framework is expected to yield a 30–50% improvement in accuracy, the exact quantitative improvement and the precise separation of lattice versus electronic contributions remain subject to experimental validation. There is some uncertainty, particularly in regimes where subtle interactions between carriers occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled oxygen content (<1 wt%) and measure the lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity separately over the 300–1200 K temperature range using methods such as inelastic neutron/X-ray scattering for phonon characterization and electronic transport spectroscopy. Apply the new predictive framework to generate separate conductivity predictions and compare with experimental measurements.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity (via Green–Kubo MD and phonon lifetime analysis)
Electronic thermal conductivity (via DFT-based Boltzmann transport and relaxation time estimation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the framework’s predicted values for either the lattice or the electronic contribution (or their sum) deviate by more than ±15% from the corresponding experimental measurements, or if the overall predictive improvement relative to traditional conflated methods is less than approximately 30%, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As mentioned in the introduction, it is worth comparing the vibrational dynamics of our HEA to glasses and to crystalline materials with very large unit cells (CMAs), to identify similarities and differences and establish the place of HEAs with respect to these classes of materials. Specifically, as previously said, the low and weakly temperature dependent thermal conductivity in glasses has been associated to the existence of a strong phonon scattering due to the intrinsic disorder. Such regime, characterized by ΓFWHM ∝ (ℏω)4, has been reported in some glasses at energies corresponding to the deviation of the GVDOS from the Debye behavior and has lately been ascribed mostly to the force-constant disorder at a nanometric lengthscale. Interestingly, the same phenomenology arises in random matrix approaches, which model the vibrational properties of a glass through a random network of force-constants over a regular lattice, quite similarly to the case of our HEA,. It is thus important to check weather the same behavior can be found in our HEA, where force-constant fluctuations are the dominant phonon scattering source.

As the calculation of transport coefficients is very demanding in term of the band structure accuracy, a much denser, 9 × 9 × 9 k-point mesh was employed to obtain the electrons energy eigenvalues for the subsequent electronic transport properties calculation. As within the RTA the lifetime of electrons has to be determined separately, which constitutes an inherent limitation to the linearized Boltzmann transport equation approach, the relaxation time (τ) was determined using the deformation potential (DP) theory []. Due to heavy elements present in the structure, the spin–orbit coupling (SOC) effect was considered in our calculations. The lattice thermal conductivity was calculated using the Green–Kubo theory for which the heat flux was obtained from the on-the-fly machine-learned force fields [,] module of VASP. The evident advantage of using this approach is that classical molecular dynamics allows for catching the phonon dynamics at any order and is applicable to potentially extremely large structures.
